adams-apple.text: Adam's Apple is the bar side of The Tavern, which two Penn State students and WWII veterans, John O'Connor and Ralph Yeager, opened on May 12, 1948 in a building that had been storage for Harvey Brothers' Bakery. After seven expansions The Tavern spans three connected buildings — the brick one became Adam's Apple — and the walls are hung with Penn State and Pennsylvania history.
adams-apple.descriptor: The Tavern Restaurant's bar, in a brick building on East College Avenue

allen-street-grill.text: The Allen Street Grill opened in 1991 on the second floor of the Hotel State College, in space that had been the Corner Room's offices. The corner has hosted a business since 1855, when it was Jack's Road House, and the building was one of the first in State College to have electricity.
allen-street-grill.descriptor: Restaurant and bar above the Corner Room at College and Allen

antifragile-brewing-co.text: Opened in spring 2022 by Lisa Harpster and John Schaffer, Antifragile was the first brewery within State College borough. The name comes from Nassim Nicholas Taleb's book about things that gain from disorder — a fit, the owners said, for fermentation. They also pour Moody Culture kombucha, the label they launched in 2017, alongside IPAs, pale ales, stouts, lagers and saisons.
antifragile-brewing-co.descriptor: Downtown's first brewery and taproom, on East Calder Way since 2022

as-pub.text: Opened in June 2018, A's is a bar inside a grocery store: you load a prepaid card, tap it at one of about 20 taps and pour your own beer, paying by the ounce. It's named for the Agostinelli family, who own McLanahan's Downtown Market, and locals prize it for cheap drafts and live music with no cover.
as-pub.descriptor: Self-pour taproom inside McLanahan's Downtown Market on S. Allen St.

bagel-crust-beaver.text: Al Rusinque opened the first Bagel Crust at 332 E. Calder Way in late May 2014, moving to State College partly to be near his son, then a Penn State pre-med student; he had already run bagel shops in Delaware, Florida and Maryland over 22 years. The bagels are made by hand, and Rusinque, a painter, was at work on a canvas of the Corner Room to hang in the shop.
bagel-crust-beaver.descriptor: Hand-made New York-style bagels and breakfast sandwiches downtown

bagel-crust-calder.text: Bagel Crust runs two downtown State College shops — this one on East Calder Way — turning out bagels, deli sandwiches, omelets and, unusually for a bagel counter, tacos. The morning-after sandwich names are half the appeal: the "Walk of Shame" and the "Hangover."
bagel-crust-calder.descriptor: Bagel and deli counter on East Calder Way; breakfast sandwiches and tacos

beaver-stadium.text: Beaver Stadium seats 106,304, making it the second-largest stadium in the Western Hemisphere. Its predecessor, New Beaver Field, was literally dismantled and hauled half a mile east to this site for the 1960 opening. The student-born "White Out" started with a 2005 Ohio State game and now turns the entire bowl into a sea of white.
beaver-stadium.descriptor: Penn State's 106,000-seat football stadium on the east end of campus

big-bowl-noodle-house.text: A cheap, generous downtown standby for noodle soups, steamed dumplings and house special fried rice, tucked next to and underneath McLanahan's on College Avenue — it also pours boba in 33 flavors.
big-bowl-noodle-house.descriptor: Chinese-Taiwanese noodle house under McLanahan's on East College Avenue

bill-pickles-tap-room.text: The bar is named for Bill Pickle, a Prohibition-era State College character who, as the taproom tells it, kept students and alumni supplied with liquor on game days before twelve children turned him teetotaler — the venue itself allows the stories may not be true. It reopened in June 2024 after a refresh of floors and paint that also brought in a barbecue menu.
bill-pickles-tap-room.descriptor: BBQ, whiskey and cocktails bar at 106 S. Allen St.

bistrozine.text: Open since July 2018 in a Calder Way storefront that used to be a dental office, Bistrozine serves Asian-influenced dishes with a twist — specialty ramen, avocado salad, five-spice chicken, crispy pork belly — presented on a magazine-style menu with a photo of each dish. Its outdoor seating includes hanging swing chairs.
bistrozine.descriptor: Asian-fusion bistro on East Calder Way with patio swing chairs

blue-course.text: The Blue is the longer half of Penn State's two courses, laid out in the late 1960s by Harrison & Grabin — both Penn State grads — as a modern companion to the 1920s White Course next door. It plays to a par 72 at more than 7,200 yards, and after a redesign it hosted the 2009 Big Ten Men's Golf Championship and still hosts the annual Rutherford Intercollegiate.
blue-course.descriptor: Penn State's par-72 championship course on West College Ave

brothers-pizza.text: The Northland Center shop is one of three Original Brothers Pizza locations, started by Anthony Pistone — born in Sicily in 1940, in the U.S. from 1954 — and his brothers, with his son carrying it on. Dough is made daily and cheese shredded in house, and each location hangs old photos telling the family's story.
brothers-pizza.descriptor: Family pizzeria in Northland Center; dough made daily, Sicilian family recipes

bryce-jordan-center.text: The Bryce Jordan Center opened January 6, 1996 and is named for Bryce Jordan, Penn State's president from 1983 to 1990, who was instrumental in acquiring the funding to build it. Aerosmith recorded part of a live album here in 1998, and Metallica's October 2018 show set the attendance record at 15,588 — a mark a January 2023 wrestling match against Iowa later broke with 15,998.
bryce-jordan-center.descriptor: 15,000-seat arena for Penn State basketball and concerts

butterfly-garden.text: The Snetsinger Butterfly Garden was started by Penn State entomologist Robert "Butterfly Bob" Snetsinger and his wife Wendy in memory of their daughter Clare, who died at 17 — the same age as Tom Tudek, the park's namesake, who also loved butterflies. Penn State Master Gardeners partnered with Snetsinger in 2007 to expand it, and the three acres now host more than 30 resident butterfly species.
butterfly-garden.descriptor: Three-acre butterfly garden inside Tom Tudek Memorial Park

cafe-210-west.text: Cafe 210 West is best known for "55 Days of Cafe," a challenge that started in 2008: buy something off the menu every single day for 55 straight days, from the Monday after spring break to the end of the semester, and your name goes on a plaque in the bar. In a good year hundreds finish — 304 did in 2014.
cafe-210-west.descriptor: College bar on W. College Ave known for the 55 Days of Cafe challenge

cafe-laura.text: Cafe Laura is a working classroom: a "living lab" where Penn State hospitality-management students cook and run the front of house toward the 1,000 hours of professional experience their degree requires. The program behind it, founded in 1937, is one of the oldest hospitality programs in North America, and the same operation also serves the Statler Executive Dining Room.
cafe-laura.descriptor: Student-run teaching restaurant of Penn State's hospitality school

canyon-pizza.text: Canyon has been feeding the 2 a.m. bar crowd since 2001 — on football weekends the line for a slice runs out the door and down Beaver Avenue. In 2023 borough council voted to take its building by eminent domain for a parking garage, then rescinded the decision about three weeks later.
canyon-pizza.descriptor: Late-night by-the-slice pizza counter at 219 E. Beaver Ave. since 2001

centre-furnace.text: Ironmasters Samuel Miles and John Patton built Centre Furnace here in 1791 and put it "into blast" in 1792, and an ironmaking village grew up around the stack. The ironmaster's house later belonged to Moses and Mary Irvin Thompson, and it is where the first steps toward founding the school that became Penn State were taken in 1855 — the university dedicated a "Birthplace of Penn State" marker on the grounds in 2024.
centre-furnace.descriptor: 1791 charcoal iron furnace and ironmaster's mansion, now a house museum

centre-furnace-mansion.text: Built in 1830 as the ironmaster's house at Centre Furnace — the first charcoal iron furnace west of the Susquehanna, built in 1790-91 and the namesake of Centre County — the mansion is tied to the 19th-century beginnings of Penn State. Moses Thompson's family lived here from 1842 to 1891; it's now the Centre County Historical Society's headquarters, listed on the National Register since 1979.
centre-furnace-mansion.descriptor: 1830 ironmaster's mansion and furnace stack; Centre County Historical Society HQ

centre-hills-country-club.text: Thirteen residents — business leaders plus Penn State faculty and administrators — founded Centre Hills in 1921, buying 65 acres of farmland near Lemont for $6,000. The original nine was designed by Alexander Findlay, often called the "Father of American Golf." In May 1953 President Dwight Eisenhower played here while visiting his brother, Penn State president Milton Eisenhower, and club records say he was the first to use the new fourth tee.
centre-hills-country-club.descriptor: Private 27-hole country club founded in 1921, near Lemont

champs-downtown.text: Champ's is the big-screen sports-bar end of the Allen Street strip, showing NFL, NBA, NCAA and NHL games until 2 a.m. and doubling as a DJ and events room. It's also the host of "Townie Takeover," a locals-first summer kickoff that hands downtown back to the residents for an evening.
champs-downtown.descriptor: Sports bar and DJ venue at 139 S. Allen St.

champs-sports-grill.descriptor: Sports bar and grill on N. Atherton St in State College

chew-chew-bun.text: Skye Chang, a former Penn State math student who returned to town in 2018 and found nowhere to buy Asian pastries, started Chew Chew Bun with his mother, Jenny Tsai — a baker with more than 20 years in Chinese and Japanese kitchens — as head baker. The Taiwanese-style melon bun is the bestseller; Chang's own pick is the garlic cheese pull bun. It moved from the Nittany Mall to 115 E. Beaver Ave. in August 2022.
chew-chew-bun.descriptor: Taiwanese-style bakery on E. Beaver Ave known for its melon buns

chumleys.text: Chumley's opened in 1984, started by Liz Pierce and Joe Schrantz serving soup, sandwiches and beer to a professional crowd, and became State College's LGBTQ+ bar — unusual for the era in that it took a visible storefront on a main downtown corner instead of hiding. The windows were dark at first and newcomers hesitated outside; a 2021 renovation opened them up and added artistic touches.
chumleys.descriptor: LGBTQ+ bar at 108 W. College Ave., open since 1984

college-buffet.descriptor: Chinese buffet and wok kitchen at 1631 N. Atherton St

cozy-thai.text: Cozy Thai is at 232 S. Allen Street, and it splits its day in an unusual way: self-service dine-in at lunch, full table service at dinner.
cozy-thai.descriptor: Thai restaurant at 232 S. Allen St., self-serve at lunch, full service at dinner

discovery-space.text: A nonprofit science center envisioned in 2002 by the Downtown State College Improvement District and established in 2007, it acquired and opened its first home at 112 W. Foster Ave. in 2010-11, then relocated to the larger North Atherton space in 2017. It runs camps and traveling exhibits alongside its hands-on STEM exhibits, plus a makerspace called The Rivet.
discovery-space.descriptor: Hands-on children's science center at 1224 N. Atherton Street

doggies-pub.text: Doggie's took over the space that held the All-American Rathskeller, which opened just after Prohibition ended and ran more than 80 years before closing in January 2018. Owners Tom and Kelley Trosko named it in homage to a former Skeller proprietor, then dropped "Rathskeller" from the name amid a trademark suit from the previous owners. The beer garden and cheap late-night pizza slices are the draw.
doggies-pub.descriptor: Pub, pizza and beer garden at 108 S. Pugh St.

elxir-coffee-roasters.text: Elixr is a Philadelphia roaster, founded in 2010 and known for lighter-roasted coffees, and its shop at 123 W. Beaver Ave is the only Elixr location in Pennsylvania outside Philadelphia.
elxir-coffee-roasters.descriptor: Philly roaster Elixr's light-roast coffee bar at 123 W. Beaver Ave

ems-museum-and-art-gallery.text: Its collection dates to 1859, when the Pennsylvania legislature handed one of four state mineralogical and geological cabinets to the Farmers' High School that became Penn State. Today it holds roughly 19,000 earth materials — rocks, minerals, fossils, meteorites — plus 4,500 historic tools of scientific research and the 325-piece Steidle Collection of American Industrial Art, largely Depression-era works celebrating Pennsylvania industry and its workers.
ems-museum-and-art-gallery.descriptor: Geology, mining and industrial-art museum in Penn State's Deike Building

faccia-luna.text: Faccia Luna has been at 1229 S. Atherton St. since 1991, run by Bill McFadden, a local restaurateur since the 1970s. Away from the downtown strip, it is known for 14 varieties of wood-fired pizza in three sizes each, Italian seafood plates such as P.E.I. mussels marinière, and house-made cannoli.
faccia-luna.descriptor: Wood-fired pizzeria and Italian kitchen on S. Atherton St. since 1991

famous-ernies-steaks.text: Named for Ernie Oelbermann, a WWII B-17 pilot with a master's in physics who ran The Phyrst next door from 1968 to 2000 and led the Phyrst Phamily singalongs that became a Penn State ritual. He died in 2015 at 90, and the cheesesteak counter on East Beaver Avenue still carries his name.
famous-ernies-steaks.descriptor: Cheesesteak counter at 111 E. Beaver Ave, next door to The Phyrst

federal-taphouse.text: Penn State alumni Corey Fogarty and Judd Goodman brought their Federal Taphouse chain to State College in July 2017, taking the second floor of the then-new Fraser Centre alongside a Hyatt Place hotel. It pours 100 craft beers and 10 wines on tap, and the scratch kitchen turns out house-made pretzels and pickles plus pizzas from an Italian oven imported and assembled on site.
federal-taphouse.descriptor: Craft-beer taphouse on the second floor of downtown's Fraser Centre

fiddlehead.text: Fiddlehead opened on West College Avenue in January 2012 in the old Chocolate Madness space, started by the Schoenholtz family, who also run Irving's downtown. The pitch then and now: build-your-own salads and grain bowls from 40-plus ingredients with dressings made in house — food the owners said was "missing or underrepresented downtown."
fiddlehead.descriptor: Build-your-own salad and grain bowl counter on W. College Ave since 2012

fuji-jade-garden-my-thai.descriptor: Chinese and Thai menus in one Northland Center storefront

green-bowl.text: Green Bowl is a West Beaver Avenue spot specializing in Xi'an cooking, with noodles made fresh daily — braised beef noodles in chili oil, cold sesame noodles, hot-and-sour beef noodles and roujiamo meat sandwiches.
green-bowl.descriptor: Xi'an-style fresh noodle shop on West Beaver Avenue

happy-valley-brewing-company.text: Happy Valley Brewing opened in fall 2013 inside a 200-year-old barn on Elmwood Street toward Lemont, and the barn is the whole idea — beer brewed on site, pub food built on seasonal local ingredients, live music in the lower bar. "If we didn't believe for this barn to be revitalized, we wouldn't be here," the general manager said as the brewery marked ten years in 2023.
happy-valley-brewing-company.descriptor: Brewpub in a 200-year-old barn on Elmwood Street, open since 2013

hiway-pizza-pub.text: The Zangrilli family opened HiWay Pizza on Hiester Street in 1963; the original shop later moved to North Atherton, and this West College Avenue pub opened in November 2017 — the owners said it felt good to be "back in the neighborhood." Now run by Dante's Restaurants, it serves five house-made dough styles, including the trademark flaky crust behind the Vodka Flaky with prosciutto.
hiway-pizza-pub.descriptor: State College pizza pub serving HiWay's pies since 1963, W College Ave

ho-smith-botanic-gardens.text: The H.O. Smith Botanic Gardens are the centerpiece of Penn State's Arboretum — about 10 acres of themed gardens plus 14 acres of meadows and paths. They opened in fall 2009 and were dedicated in April 2010, built with a $10 million gift from Charles "Skip" Smith, who named them for his father. The Childhood's Gate Children's Garden followed in 2014 and a three-acre Pollinator and Bird Garden in 2021.
ho-smith-botanic-gardens.descriptor: 10 acres of themed gardens at the Penn State Arboretum, opened 2009

hosss-steak-sea-house.text: Hoss's is a Pennsylvania-born steakhouse chain founded in 1983 and still nearly all in-state — 29 of its 30 restaurants are in Pennsylvania, plus one in West Virginia. The draw is steaks, chicken and seafood cooked to order alongside a soup, salad, bread and dessert bar with more than 100 items, and the chain makes a point of not charging extra for butter, gravy, sour cream, fried onions or sauces.
hosss-steak-sea-house.descriptor: Pennsylvania steak-and-seafood chain on N Atherton with a 100-item salad bar

india-pavilion.text: India Pavilion has served North Indian food at 222 E. Calder Way since 1997, grinding its own spices and making paneer and yogurt from scratch. It holds no liquor license, so it's BYOB with no cork charge, and there's an all-you-can-eat lunch buffet with vegetarian and non-vegetarian selections.
india-pavilion.descriptor: BYOB North Indian kitchen on East Calder Way with a lunch buffet, since 1997

irvings-bagels.descriptor: Bagel and bread bakery cafe at 110 E. College Ave.

kamrai-thai-sushi.text: Kamrai serves Thai food and sushi out of a Victorian manor house on Pike Street in Lemont, the village at the foot of Mount Nittany, and it's BYOB. When the owners opened a spin-off, Maxx Sushi & Ramen, down the street in April 2019, they said they would keep Kamrai exactly as it is and put the ramen on the new menu instead.
kamrai-thai-sushi.descriptor: Thai and sushi BYOB in a Victorian house on Pike Street in Lemont

lion-shrine.text: Sculptor Heinz Warneke carved the Nittany Lion from a 13-ton block of Indiana limestone, and it was dedicated at homecoming on October 24, 1942 as the class of 1940's gift. Vandals have broken off its right ear more than once — in 1978, 1997, 2003 and 2018.
lion-shrine.descriptor: Limestone Nittany Lion carving near Rec Hall, the class of 1940's gift

lionne.text: Lionne, styled Lionne American Brasserie, is the fine-dining room of the Nittany Lion Inn, the campus hotel built in 1931. It opened as the inn reopened on Sept. 3, 2024, after 16 months of construction. Executive chef Mirko Loeffler, who began training in southern Germany in the mid-1970s, built a menu of fresh, seasonal dishes with French Mediterranean influence — including the signature Lionne salad of Maine lobster, duck confit and butternut squash.
lionne.descriptor: Fine dining in the 1931 Nittany Lion Inn, Mediterranean with French accents

lions-den.text: The Lion's Den, at 118 S. Garner St., calls itself a legendary Happy Valley bar and dates itself to 1959. It runs house DJs and a dance floor for the Penn State late-night crowd, and stays open into the early morning hours.
lions-den.descriptor: Late-night DJ and dance bar on South Garner Street

little-szechuan.text: Little Szechuan opened on West College Avenue in December 2013 and expanded in 2015 to seat about 90. Husband-and-wife owners Tao Xu, the head chef, and Sharon Ngan run it, and the kitchen leans real Szechuan rather than Americanized Chinese — pork dumplings in hot chili, double-cooked pork, hot pot, and live tilapia and lobster. Xu is from Chengdu; as Ngan describes it, the Szechuan peppercorn brings a tingly, numbing sensation.
little-szechuan.descriptor: Szechuan restaurant at 228 W College Ave, open since 2013

local-whiskey.text: Local Whiskey sits above The Phyrst at 107 E. Beaver Ave. and calls itself State College's premier whiskey bar — a long whiskey list, live acoustic sets on weeknights, late-night food, and standing deals like 20% off whiskey on Wednesdays. It belongs to the same local restaurant group as The Phyrst, Champs and Central Reservation.
local-whiskey.descriptor: Whiskey bar above The Phyrst on East Beaver Ave., with live music

lubrano-park.text: Medlar Field at Lubrano Park opened in June 2006 beside Beaver Stadium and is shared by Penn State baseball and the State College Spikes. It was deliberately designed so Mount Nittany rises unobstructed beyond the outfield wall. Its dimensions mirror Pittsburgh's PNC Park with one exception: the right-field wall stands 18.55 feet instead of 21 — a nod to Penn State's 1855 founding.
lubrano-park.descriptor: 5,570-seat ballpark by Beaver Stadium; Penn State baseball and the Spikes

lupitas-authentic-mexican-food.text: Maria Guadalupe "Lupita" Rojas Orozco and Emilio Lopez Ramirez came from San Dionisio del Mar, Oaxaca, and after arriving in central Pennsylvania to work on farms she began phoning her mother in Mexico for recipes. Home cooking became a food truck, then a counter inside a Uni-Mart at Whitehall Road and West College Avenue in June 2019, where handmade corn tortillas are pressed daily.
lupitas-authentic-mexican-food.descriptor: Oaxacan taqueria on W. Beaver Ave; handmade tortillas, sopes, gorditas

maine-bay-berry-co.text: Co-owner Shaun Knight, a Winter Harbor, Maine native who taught at Penn State's Smeal College for 15 years, kept getting asked to bring lobster back from home. In July 2017 he and Christa Stofferahn were driving back from Maine late at night, spotted an empty produce stand on Shiloh Road and leased it, opening that August. They moved into The Barn at Lemont in January 2018; Knight still drives to Maine three or four times a month.
maine-bay-berry-co.descriptor: Maine seafood market and lobster rolls at The Barn at Lemont on Elmwood St

martin-luther-king-jr-memorial.text: State College dedicated its Martin Luther King Jr. Plaza on Aug. 28, 2017, the 54th anniversary of the March on Washington. Granite pavers set into the walkway mark milestones in King's life and in local Black history, and a graphic wall enlarges photographs of King's Jan. 21, 1965 speech at Penn State's Rec Hall. Pillars at Fraser and Beaver carry his philosophies.
martin-luther-king-jr-memorial.descriptor: Civil-rights memorial plaza on Fraser Street, dedicated in 2017

marzonis-brick-oven-brewing-co.text: The Altoona-area chain, founded in 2003, opened this fifth central-Pennsylvania location on Sept. 5, 2023, at 1215 N. Atherton St., in a building that had sat vacant since TGI Friday's left in 2020. Seven signature beers brewed at Marzoni's Blair County brewery are poured alongside brick-oven pizzas, pastas, steaks and seafood.
marzonis-brick-oven-brewing-co.descriptor: Brick-oven pizza and house-brewed beer on N. Atherton St. since 2023

masala-palace.descriptor: Indian kitchen at 120 E. Beaver Ave; tikka masala, butter chicken, biryani

medlar-field-at-lubrano-park.text: Opened in June 2006, Medlar Field was laid out on essentially the same playing-field footprint as PNC Park in Pittsburgh — the right-field wall is the exception, at 18.55 feet for Penn State's 1855 founding — and it was designed so Mount Nittany sits in an unobstructed view over the outfield wall. It's shared by Penn State's Nittany Lions and the minor league State College Spikes.
medlar-field-at-lubrano-park.descriptor: 5,570-seat ballpark for Penn State baseball and the State College Spikes

millbrook-marsh-nature-center.text: Millbrook Marsh covers 62 acres off Puddintown Road, roughly 50 of them wetland, crossed by a boardwalk that lets visitors walk out into the marsh. Its wetlands slow flooding and filter water heading into Spring Run, Thompson Run and Slab Cabin Run and eventually the Chesapeake Bay. Centre Region Parks and Recreation runs the center, a restored bank barn anchors the site, and a ClearWater Conservancy easement with Penn State keeps the marsh from being developed.
millbrook-marsh-nature-center.descriptor: 62-acre wetland preserve with a boardwalk off Puddintown Road

nittany-lion-softball-park.text: Penn State softball's home opened on March 26, 2011 as a $10.2 million facility with 1,084 permanent seats, lights, a press box with broadcast booths, and an adjacent softball-only building holding locker rooms and training space. The playing surface is Beard Field, named for Lee and William Beard after their $500,000 gift to the project in October 2009.
nittany-lion-softball-park.descriptor: Penn State softball's 1,084-seat campus ballpark, opened 2011

old-botany.text: Old Botany is the oldest standing building with its original facade on Penn State's University Park campus and was the original home of the university's botany department. Ghost lore says Frances Atherton, wife of president George Atherton, can be seen at a window watching over her husband's grave — and that a spirit torments those who stay too late, rolling up carpets and shattering glass.
old-botany.descriptor: Penn State's oldest building with its original facade, on the University Park campus

old-main.text: The first Old Main was finished in 1863; after being judged structurally unsound in the 1920s it was razed in 1929 and rebuilt on the same footprint, reopening in 1930. Its second floor holds Henry Varnum Poor's Land-Grant Frescoes, roughly 1,300 square feet painted between 1940 and 1949, and the tower bell — cast in 1871 — was a gift of the class of 1904.
old-main.descriptor: Penn State's 1930 administration building and campus bell tower

original-waffle-shop.text: Greek immigrant John Dimakopoulos opened his first Waffle Shop downtown and ran the family's shops on a "fresh, fast and fun" credo for 52 years before selling to Chris and Michelle Paret in January 2025. This North Atherton shop and its West College Avenue sibling are breakfast-and-lunch only, closing at 3 p.m., with omelets and waffles the headliners.
original-waffle-shop.descriptor: Breakfast-and-lunch diner at 1229 N. Atherton St. — omelets, waffles, cheesesteaks

palmer-museum-at-the-arboretum.text: Penn State's Palmer Museum left its Brutalist campus building for a new 73,000-square-foot Allied Works home at the Arboretum in 2023, nearly doubling its exhibition space. Admission is free, and the museum bills its holdings — nearly 11,000 works — as the largest art museum collection between Pittsburgh and Philadelphia.
palmer-museum-at-the-arboretum.descriptor: Free Penn State art museum at the Arboretum, 650 Bigler Road

penang.descriptor: Malaysian and Southeast Asian fusion on N. Atherton St; roti canai, char kuey teow

penn-state-all-sports-museum.text: Opened in February 2002 near Gate B of Beaver Stadium, in the stadium's southwest corner, the museum covers every Penn State varsity sport plus the Blue Band, the cheerleaders and the students who have worn the Nittany Lion suit. Its best-known artifact is John Cappelletti's Heisman Trophy; a Lego model of Beaver Stadium built from 7,647 bricks is a newer draw.
penn-state-all-sports-museum.descriptor: Penn State athletics museum inside Beaver Stadium, open since 2002

pennsylvania-state-golf-courses.text: Penn State's golf dates to 1921, when professors Bob Rutherford and R.D. Pryde laid out nine holes on campus; architect Willie Park Jr. added nine more, completed by 1926, to finish what is now the White Course. A second, longer layout — the Blue — followed in the late 1960s, and a 1990s master plan retrofitted both courses around a new shared clubhouse that opened in 1994. Together they host Penn State's varsity golf teams and public play.
pennsylvania-state-golf-courses.descriptor: Penn State's 36 holes on W College Ave: the 1920s White and longer Blue

phyrst.text: Opened in 1967, the Phyrst still has the stained-glass windows and 10-foot medieval door its original owners built. Its house band, the Phyrst Phamily, made Saturday night sing-alongs a State College institution for decades, and the walls are papered with 21st-birthday photos.
phyrst.descriptor: Sing-along bar on E. Beaver Ave. with a house band, since 1967

pita-cabana.text: A halal Mediterranean counter owned by Hitham Hiyajneh, who also runs Yallah Taco, Underground Burger and Dulce Luca Cafe as part of a small downtown restaurant group. The menu is Lebanese-inspired — fattoush, lentil soup, gyro platters, shawarma — with vegetarian and vegan options throughout.
pita-cabana.descriptor: Halal Lebanese-inspired pita, gyro and shawarma spot on East Calder Way

robeson-gallery.text: One of the HUB-Robeson Galleries on the first floor of Penn State's student union, showing rotating contemporary exhibitions by student, local and visiting artists — free and open to all, Monday through Friday. The building's Robeson half was renamed in 1986 for Paul Robeson, in recognition of his contributions to the civil rights movement.
robeson-gallery.descriptor: Free contemporary-art gallery inside Penn State's HUB-Robeson Center

rothrock-coffee.text: Rothrock Coffee takes its name from Rothrock State Forest — the roasters say it came out of "countless caffeine fueled bike rides" in those mountains, and the cycling theme runs through blends named Singlespeed, Trailside and Gravel Road. In 2023 the local roastery landed its K-cups in about 300 Walmart stores from Maine to North Carolina.
rothrock-coffee.descriptor: Local specialty coffee roaster and cafe named for Rothrock State Forest

sakura-asian-restaurant.descriptor: Sushi bar and hibachi kitchen at 1525 S. Atherton St

sharkies-bar.text: Known for years as "Sharkies Pool Bar" for its tables, the Sowers Street bar reinvented itself in summer 2025 — turning its parking lot into a patio with TVs and lawn games, making the basement non-smoking, and rebranding from "Pool Bar" to "Cool Bar" while leaning into karaoke, DJs, trivia and live music.
sharkies-bar.descriptor: Longtime pool-hall bar on Sowers Street with a big outdoor patio

sher-halal-gyro.text: It began as a halal cart parked on East Beaver Avenue behind 3 Dots, serving rice platters with chicken, lamb, shrimp or fish alongside gyros, falafel and wings. The cart did well enough that in 2024 Sher announced a downtown storefront at 145 S. Allen St., taking the space Woodring's Floral Gardens had occupied for 46 years.
sher-halal-gyro.descriptor: Halal cart on E. Beaver Ave — gyros, falafel and rice platters

sidney-friedman-park.text: The block held the Frazier Street School, built in 1897 as State College's second schoolhouse, until it closed in 1955; the Post Office bought two-thirds and the borough leased the rest, opening it as Central Parklet in 1966. It was renamed in 2009 for Sidney Friedman, the developer who bought the Corner Room, Hotel State College and the Cathaum, created Calder Square, and donated the State Theatre to Penn State.
sidney-friedman-park.descriptor: Downtown pocket park on S. Fraser St, home to summer movie nights

slab-cabin-park.text: Twenty acres of hiking and biking trails in College Township, about five minutes out of town toward Lemont, best known for a sledding hill local coverage calls "easily 300 feet from top to bottom" — so popular that the park had to post a list of sledding rules, and Penn State students have piled onto it for years. A covered bridge links the trail system, and there's a public fire pit at the top of the hill.
slab-cabin-park.descriptor: College Township regional park with hiking trails and a big sledding hill

snap-custom-pizza.text: Snap began in the mid-1990s when two friends, Peter Howey and Aaron Nocks, started making pizzas for themselves and the Villanova rowing team. It's now an eight-location chain across Pennsylvania and Delaware that makes its own dough and cheese every day, with each pie built to order.
snap-custom-pizza.descriptor: Build-your-own pizza counter; dough and cheese made fresh daily

south-food-district.text: Penn State organizes campus dining into food districts, and the South Food District is centered on Redifer Commons in South Halls, home to the Redifer City Grill. A spring-break remodel gave the dining hall two hot lines and expanded the salad bar at the back, relieving the congestion around the old beverage station.
south-food-district.descriptor: Penn State dining commons in Redifer Hall, serving the South Halls dorms

sowers-harvest-cafe.text: Sowers Harvest is a mission-driven cafe — part of the Extend Cafes network — that describes its aim as creating "a peaceful space around coffee and cuisine to cultivate conversations that change the world." It leans on fresh, locally sourced ingredients and hosts cultural nights and conversation workshops alongside the omelets and lattes.
sowers-harvest-cafe.descriptor: Healthy breakfast-and-lunch cafe on East Beaver Avenue

stage-west.text: Opened in February 2020 by Steve Masterson, Stage West bills itself as downtown's only real live-music venue outside the Bryce Jordan Center and the State Theatre, booking a different genre most nights. It took over an address that had chewed through bars: Crowbar closed there in 2006, followed by RE//BAR, Envy, Levels and Mezzanine.
stage-west.descriptor: Live-music bar and nightclub at 420 E. College Ave.

state-theatre.text: Warner Bros. built the State as a $70,000 cinema, opening in 1938 with "The Sisters," starring Errol Flynn and Bette Davis. It ran films until March 2001, then sat dark until a community-led renovation reopened it in December 2006 as a 554-seat nonprofit venue for music, film, dance and theater.
state-theatre.descriptor: 1938 movie house at 130 W. College Ave, now a nonprofit performing arts venue

tadashi-japanese-restaurant.text: When Tadashi opened on College Avenue it was a rarity for State College — an izakaya-style Japanese restaurant built around ramen and yakitori skewers rather than sushi and teriyaki, with tako wasabi and chicken-gizzard and quail-egg skewers on the menu. Owner Jerry Gao opened a second downtown location in The Metropolitan in 2019, saying simply that "the old place is too small."
tadashi-japanese-restaurant.descriptor: Izakaya-style Japanese spot downtown known for ramen and yakitori

the-arboretum-at-penn-state.text: The arboretum's first tree, a white oak, was dedicated in 2005, and the H.O. Smith Botanic Gardens were dedicated on April 25, 2010, funded by a $10 million gift from Charles "Skip" Smith. The Childhood's Gate Children's Garden opened in 2014, and the rebuilt Palmer Museum of Art opened next door in June 2024.
the-arboretum-at-penn-state.descriptor: 370-acre campus arboretum with the H.O. Smith Botanic Gardens

the-brewery.text: The Brewery has been in the basement at 233 E. Beaver Ave., at the corner of McAllister Alley, since the late 1960s — one of its owners calls it "the four-star dive behind the dumpsters." On August 7, 2023 the borough council voted to take the building by eminent domain for a parking garage, then rescinded the motion at its August 21 meeting after a petition and hours of public testimony.
the-brewery.descriptor: Basement dive bar and live-music room off McAllister Alley since the 1960s

the-cheese-shoppe.text: Bill Clarke opened The Cheese Shoppe on East Calder Way on February 19, 1977. When cheese sales sagged he added in-store coffee roasting, saying he was "one of the first six in-store roasters on the East Coast," and he now ships coffee to customers in more than 30 states.
the-cheese-shoppe.descriptor: Gourmet cheese shop and in-house coffee roaster on Calder Way since 1977

the-corner-room.text: The Corner Room opened on August 2, 1926 inside the newly renamed Hotel State College, and it has never budged from its corner — it marked its 100th year in 2026. The site fed travelers long before that: in the mid-1800s it was Jack's Road House, where a dollar a day bought lodging and meals.
the-corner-room.descriptor: All-day American restaurant at College Ave and Allen St since 1926

the-frost-entomological-museum.text: Penn State's insect museum holds well over a million arthropod specimens, some collected in the late 1800s — including the Beatty collection's 60,000-plus dragonflies and damselflies and more than 32,000 mounted aphids. Founded in 1969 and named for entomologist Stuart W. Frost, it's open to the public and runs an annual Hexapod Haiku Challenge.
the-frost-entomological-museum.descriptor: Penn State insect museum with a million-plus specimens, on the Ag campus

the-land-grant-frescoes.text: Muralist Henry Varnum Poor painted these straight onto wet plaster in Old Main's lobby — his daughter Anne applied a fresh section each morning so the pigment became part of the wall itself. The 1940 north-wall panel shows Abraham Lincoln and a student planting a tree, a nod to the 1862 Morrill Land-Grant Act; wing panels of mining, farming and classroom life were added in 1948. The 1,300-square-foot work was restored in 2014.
the-land-grant-frescoes.descriptor: 1,300 sq ft of 1940s fresco murals in Penn State's Old Main lobby

the-original-waffle-shop-west.text: The West College shop served 99,808 omelets and 32,532 waffles in the first half of 2024 alone. Founder John Dimakopoulos, who came from Greece at 16 with $20 in his pocket, sold the family's East College and Bellefonte shops in 2004 to concentrate on this one and North Atherton, then sold both in January 2025 after 52 years.
the-original-waffle-shop-west.descriptor: Breakfast-and-lunch counter at 1610 W. College Ave., Ferguson Township

the-shandygaff.text: Owner Mark Sapia closes the Shandygaff every State Patty's Day, the student-invented drinking holiday, and has done so since its early years regardless of financial incentives. He backed the students at first, then decided he wanted to be "part of the solution, not the problem."
the-shandygaff.descriptor: Late-night bar known for flavored liquor pitchers and Wednesday karaoke

the-tavern.text: Two World War II veterans studying at Penn State on the GI Bill, John "Jace" O'Connor and Ralph Yeager, opened The Tavern in 1948. It rambles through three connected buildings with much older lives — the white house on College Avenue took in lodgers from 1890 and the red one went up as stables in the early 1900s — and the rooms are still furnished with period antiques and artwork.
the-tavern.descriptor: Antique-filled American restaurant at 220 E. College Ave since 1948

the-waffle-shop.text: The Waffle Shop name started downtown under Greek immigrant John Dimakopoulos, who sold the East College Avenue and Bellefonte shops in 2004 to focus on his two Original Waffle Shops; the downtown room has run under separate ownership since, paired with the Bellefonte location. A fire in October 2023 left heavy smoke damage and closed it for nearly a month.
the-waffle-shop.descriptor: Downtown breakfast counter at 364 E. College Ave., open 7 a.m. to 2 p.m.

tom-tudek-memorial-park.text: At 91 acres, Tudek is the most frequently visited park in the Centre Region, with a dog park, community gardens, playground, pavilions and a 1.3-mile loop. It is named for Tom Tudek, who died at 17 and loved butterflies — fitting, since the three-acre Snetsinger Butterfly Garden inside it was created by Robert "Butterfly Bob" and Wendy Snetsinger to honor their daughter Clare, who also died at 17. Over 30 butterfly species live there.
tom-tudek-memorial-park.descriptor: 91-acre park on Herman Drive with a dog park and a butterfly garden

tudek-dog-park.text: The park is named for Tom Tudek, who died at 17; the Snetsinger Butterfly Garden inside it is a memorial to Clare Snetsinger, who also died at 17 and shared his love of butterflies. At 91 acres — with the butterfly garden, community gardens, a playground and a 1.3-mile loop alongside the dog park — it is the most frequently visited park in the Centre Region.
tudek-dog-park.descriptor: Fenced dog park inside 91-acre Tom Tudek Memorial Park off Herman Drive

uncle-chens.descriptor: Restaurant on East Calder Way downtown, dine-in and takeout

walnut-springs-park.text: A wooded strip along Walnut Springs Lane in the Vallamont neighborhood, its trails tie the Easterly and Westerly Parkway corridor to East College Avenue and lead on toward College Township's Thompson Woods Preserve. In 2023 State College won a roughly $79,000 PennDOT grant to build a new pedestrian bridge on the route — the only Centre County award in that round.
walnut-springs-park.descriptor: Wooded borough park and trail link in the Vallamont neighborhood

waring-square.text: Waring Commons, the West Halls building it sits in, is not named for bandleader Fred Waring, as most people assume — it honors his ancestor William G. Waring, the English horticulturist hired in 1856 as the Farmers' High School's first administrator. He laid out the original campus grounds and planted the "Old Willow" that stood as a Penn State landmark for more than 60 years.
waring-square.descriptor: Campus eatery in Waring Commons, Penn State's West Halls

websters-bookstore-cafe.text: Elaine Meder-Wilgus has run Webster's since 1995, and it works as much like a commons as a bookstore-cafe: free meeting space for local groups, a platform for area musicians, poets and artists, produce from local farmers since 2004, and a Sunday brunch that went fully plant-based in 2018. She won the 2024 Madison Award for Civility in the Community for that record.
websters-bookstore-cafe.descriptor: Used-book shop and cafe at 133 E. Beaver Ave. with a Sunday vegan brunch

white-course.text: Penn State's original course dates to the 1920s: professors Bob Rutherford and R.D. Pryde laid out the first nine holes and World Golf Hall of Fame architect Willie Park Jr. designed the rest, with holes 6 through 14 still his work. A teenage Arnold Palmer won a PIAA state high school championship on it in the 1940s.
white-course.descriptor: Penn State's older golf course, with nine holes laid out by Willie Park Jr.

yallah-taco.text: Hitham Hiyajneh opened this hole-in-the-wall taco stand in a downtown alley in 2016, pitching "authentic Mexican flavors with a Mediterranean twist." The food is halal, and the tiny shack drew crowds late into the night before a larger second location opened in the former downtown Taco Bell at 310 E. College Ave. in 2020.
yallah-taco.descriptor: Halal Mexican-Mediterranean taco stand in a downtown alley

yogurt-express.descriptor: Self-serve frozen yogurt and smoothie bowls on East College Avenue

zenos-pub.text: Zeno and Chris Papadopoulos bought the Hotel State College property in 1971, found an unused liquor license in an old desk, and opened Zeno's the next year. Its 1980s "beer passport" put 80 beers from around the world in front of a college town, and it became one of the first bars on the East Coast to pour cask-conditioned beer — all from a spot "directly above the center of the earth."
zenos-pub.descriptor: Craft-beer and live-music pub at 100 W. College Ave., since 1972
